client: I started this new marketing job about six weeks ago, and honestly, I'm not sure I made the right decision taking it. Everyone around me seems so confident and experienced, and I constantly feel like I'm just waiting to be found out as someone who doesn't belong there. I've been losing sleep over deadlines and second-guessing every single piece of work I put out, and I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change any of that.
therapist: What you're describing — that constant bracing for the moment someone "finds you out" — sounds exhausting, and I can hear in how you're speaking that this is weighing on you more heavily than your words alone might suggest. What you're experiencing has a name: impostor syndrome, and it's remarkably common among capable people stepping into new challenges, which means those feelings of not belonging aren't necessarily evidence that you *don't* belong. I'm glad you're talking about it, because while it won't instantly erase the sleepless nights, it's the first step toward examining whether the story you're telling yourself about your place there actually holds up to the evidence.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I've heard of impostor syndrome before, and part of me wants to believe that's all it is, but another part of me keeps thinking — what if in my case it's actually true? Like, what if everyone else really does know things I don't, and I'm not just being hard on myself but actually seeing the situation clearly? It feels risky to just dismiss the feeling as a cognitive distortion when it might be useful information.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quick, pitched with a kind of urgency — tells me this isn't just an abstract philosophical question for you, it's something that's genuinely unsettling to sit with. And you're actually raising a really important CBT point: feelings *can* carry useful information, so the goal isn't to dismiss them, but to examine them like a scientist would — asking "what's the actual evidence, and am I weighing it fairly?" The question worth exploring together is whether you're applying the same rigorous scrutiny to evidence that you *do* belong — your hiring, any positive feedback, tasks you've completed — as you are to the fears that you don't.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess when I try to think about the evidence that I do belong, I can come up with some things — they did hire me, and my manager said my first campaign draft was "a solid start" — but my brain immediately jumps to explaining those away, like maybe they just needed to fill the position quickly or she was just being polite. It's like the negative evidence feels so much more real and heavy than the positive stuff, even when I try to line them up side by side. I'm not sure I trust myself to be a fair scientist about my own situation.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but very fast, like your mind is racing ahead even as your voice stays quiet — makes me think part of you already senses something important in what you just said. What you're describing is called the **discounting the positive** pattern, where the brain applies a much higher burden of proof to good evidence than to bad, and noticing that bias *is* actually you being a fair scientist — because an unfair one wouldn't even question whether the scales were tilted. So rather than trusting your conclusions right now, what if we just practiced noticing, together, each time your mind reaches for an explanation that conveniently erases the positive evidence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think I understand what you're suggesting, but honestly, the "noticing" part sounds easier in a therapy session than it does at 11pm when I'm staring at a spreadsheet and my brain is already in full panic mode. Like, in that moment, the discounting doesn't feel like a bias — it feels like just being realistic, and I'm not sure I'd even recognize it happening. How do you actually catch yourself doing something that feels completely natural and true?
therapist: That very high, soft, fast quality in your voice tells me you're genuinely wrestling with this — not just intellectually, but in a way that feels urgent and a little vulnerable. You've actually just identified something really important: the best time to build the "noticing" muscle isn't at 11pm in panic mode, it's now, in calmer moments like this one, so that you're creating a kind of mental bookmark — something like "when I catch myself finding a reason why the good evidence doesn't count, that's the pattern" — so it becomes more recognizable under pressure. We could even work on a specific, simple cue phrase you could use in those late-night moments, something that interrupts the spiral just long enough to ask one question rather than trying to overhaul your thinking all at once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: A cue phrase sounds simple enough in theory, but I worry that in the moment it'll just feel like a hollow thing I'm supposed to say to myself, like a pep talk that I don't actually believe. I've tried things like that before — telling myself to "just breathe" or "it'll be fine" — and it kind of bounces off when the anxiety is already running hot. I guess I'm skeptical that a few words are going to cut through something that feels this loud and convincing.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice, even as you're describing something that feels almost deflating, tells me this skepticism comes from real experience — you've *tried* to talk yourself down before and it didn't work, so this isn't resistance, it's honest feedback worth taking seriously. You're absolutely right that reassurance phrases fail because they try to argue with the anxiety, and what we'd want instead is something that doesn't claim "it'll be fine" but simply interrupts the autopilot long enough to ask one grounding question — something like "what am I treating as fact right now?" — which is less a pep talk and more a tiny wedge of curiosity. That distinction matters, because curiosity doesn't have to compete with the anxiety to be believable; it just has to create a half-second pause.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That framing actually does feel a little different — "what am I treating as fact right now" isn't telling me everything's okay, it's just asking me to look at what I'm doing, which feels less like I have to convince myself of something I don't believe. I think I could maybe try that, though I'm still not sure I'll remember it when I'm deep in a spiral at work. I guess my worry is that even if I ask the question, I'll just answer it with more catastrophizing and end up back where I started.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quick and high, with a kind of tentative energy — tells me this feels like a genuine small opening, but one you're afraid to trust too much, like you're already bracing for the moment it fails. That concern about answering the question with more catastrophizing is actually really shrewd, and it points to the next layer: the goal isn't to answer the question perfectly, it's just to notice that you *are* answering it with catastrophizing — because that recognition, even mid-spiral, is the intervention. You don't have to climb out of the hole in that moment; you just have to see that you're in one, and that small shift in perspective is genuinely different from being lost in it without knowing it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That distinction — just seeing that I'm in the hole versus having to climb out of it — actually lands differently than I expected, and I'm sitting with it for a second because it feels less impossible than what I thought you were asking me to do. But I guess I'm wondering how long it takes before that kind of noticing actually changes anything, because right now it feels like I could recognize the spiral every single night and still wake up exhausted and dreading work the next morning. I don't want to just become someone who's very aware of how anxious they are without it actually getting better.
therapist: The way you're speaking — very fast, pitched high, with a kind of breathless quality — tells me something real just shifted for you, and there's both a flicker of hope and a fear of that hope in the same breath. That concern about becoming "very aware but no better" is one of the most honest things you've said, and it's worth taking seriously: noticing *is* the mechanism of change, not just a passive observer, because each time you catch the spiral and don't fully fuse with it, you're weakening the automaticity of that pattern — it's slow, but it's not just awareness for its own sake. The exhaustion and dread won't vanish quickly, but the question worth tracking over the coming weeks isn't "did I feel anxious?" but "did the spiral have the same grip on me as before?" — because that's where the change tends to show up first.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Reframing the question that way — "did the spiral have the same grip" instead of "did I feel anxious" — actually feels like a more honest thing to measure, because I think I've been setting this impossible bar where success means not feeling anxious at all, and of course I keep failing it. But I'll be honest, six weeks in at this job with deadlines piling up, I'm not sure I have the bandwidth to also be tracking my own psychological progress on top of everything else — it feels like one more thing I could do wrong. I guess I'm worried that even this process becomes another source of pressure rather than relief.
therapist: The speed and height in your voice, even as you're describing something that sounds almost like relief mixed with exhaustion, tells me you just named something really important — that the tools meant to help you can quietly become another performance you're grading yourself on. So let's be clear: there's no tracking requirement here, no progress report, no way to do this wrong — if the only thing you take from today is that you've been measuring yourself against an impossible standard, that alone is genuinely meaningful. The goal was never to add to your load; it was to make the load you're already carrying feel a little less like evidence against you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Hearing that — that there's no way to do this wrong — actually made me exhale a little, which I didn't realize I needed. I think I've been treating even this conversation like a test I could fail, which is kind of a perfect example of exactly what we've been talking about, and there's something almost darkly funny about that. I'm not sure one session is going to quiet the voice that keeps telling me I don't belong at that job, but I think I came in expecting to feel more dismissed than I do right now.
therapist: That exhale — and the fact that you caught yourself turning *this* conversation into a test in real time, and could even laugh at it a little — is actually a meaningful moment, not a small one. You came in skeptical that talking would change anything, and while the voice telling you that you don't belong won't go quiet after one session, something shifted enough that you noticed it, and that noticing happened *here*, which means it can happen at 11pm over a spreadsheet too. I don't think you're as far from trusting yourself as you believe.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to believe that — that I'm not as far from trusting myself as I think — but there's still a part of me that wonders if I'm just feeling better because this is a safe space and you're being kind, and that the moment I'm back at my desk tomorrow it'll all collapse again. I guess what I'm sitting with is whether what happened in here is actually transferable to out there, or if it's more like a temporary relief that doesn't survive contact with the real situation. That feels like the real test, and I don't know yet if I'll pass it.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're articulating something that feels genuinely uncertain, tells me this isn't panic — it's a quiet, honest question, and it deserves a quiet, honest answer. What you're describing *is* the real test, and you're right that I can't promise it transfers — but notice that you just used everything we talked about in real time: you caught a thought, questioned whether it was fully true, and held it with some distance instead of collapsing into it, and that happened here because you did it, not because this room is magic. Tomorrow at your desk, the voice will likely be louder — but you've already proven today that you can hear it without fully believing it, and that's not something that stays behind when you leave.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
